title: Don't Shift the Trigger: Robust Gradient Ascent for Backdoor Unlearning
claim: Naive unlearning of a backdoor does not remove the trigger but redirects its influence to another class; the robust method truly removes it.
layout: 3 panels, hub-and-spoke from top center, arrows left and right, dashed divider
description: A top-center purple box shows a poisoned Llama, with example movie reviews. The trigger word 'bb' (red, underlined) correlates with a positive smiley. A thick arrow points down to a 'Poisoned Sample Detection' module, which has a clean/poison split and a red database cylinder. From it, curved purple arrows go left and right to two outcome boxes. The right box, labeled Vanilla GA, shows the unlearned model where 'bb' now correlates with the negative (sad) class, so the trigger has shifted. The left box, labeled RGA, shows the cleaned model where 'bb' is unrelated to both sentiments and predictions stay correct. Each box has negative and positive examples separated by a dashed line. Emoji sentiment labels and llama icons guide the eye. The eye goes first to the top box.
caption: Illustration of trigger shifting when applying gradient ascent to unlearn backdoors.
abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a significant threat to machine learning models, allowing adversaries to implant hidden triggers that alter model behavior when activated. Although gradient ascent (GA)-based unlearning has been proposed as an efficient backdoor removal approach, we identify a critical yet overlooked issue: vanilla GA does not eliminate the trigger but shifts its impact to different classes, a phenomenon we call trigger shifting. To address this, we propose Robust Gradient Ascent (RGA), which introduces a dynamic penalty mechanism to regulate GA's strength and prevent excessive unlearning. Our experiments show that RGA effectively removes backdoors while preserving model utility, offering a more reliable defense against backdoor attacks.
